recent_posts.title: RSS Feeds Send Me More Traffic Than Google
recent_posts.summary: A personal blog owner shares data showing that RSS/Atom feed subscribers account for roughly 25% of their traffic over the last 28 days, surpassing Google as a traffic source. Using lightweight, privacy-conscious local tracking, they found that subscribers who open posts and load images generate more visits than organic search. The author notes the data is lossy and acknowledges the two traffic types are qualitatively different, but expresses delight that so many readers choose to subscribe directly.

recent_posts.title: Vertically Aligning Roman Numerals in Code
recent_posts.summary: A PHP developer shares a trick for vertically aligning Roman numeral arrays in code. The issue is that Unicode Roman Numeral characters are not monospaced, making it impossible to align the array operators neatly. The solution is to flip the array — using integers as keys and Roman numeral strings as values, then calling array_flip() — so the numeric keys align perfectly in columns.

recent_posts.title: NHS England plans to close nearly all open source repositories over AI security fears
recent_posts.summary: NHS England is preparing to close nearly all of its open source GitHub repositories, citing security concerns related to AI-powered vulnerability scanning tools like Mythos. A former UK government technologist who championed open source across GDS, NHSX, and i.AI argues this is a gross overreaction that contradicts multiple UK government policies mandating open source by default, including the Tech Code of Practice and NHS Service Standard. The author notes the code has already been indexed by AI tools, that closing repos won't prevent AI-based attacks on binaries or live services, and that the effort to close thousands of repos is enormous for no real security gain. A Freedom of Information request has been filed, all NHS repos have been backed up, and readers are urged to contact their MPs.

recent_posts.title: Parsing .env files with PHP parse_ini_file has subtle gotchas
recent_posts.summary: PHP's built-in parse_ini_file() function can read .env files, but the two formats have subtle incompatibilities that cause silent data corruption. The .ini format uses semicolons for comments (not #), so inline # comments get included in values, semicolons inside values get truncated, double quotes in comments cause syntax errors, and exclamation points break parsing. A hacky workaround is to prefix comments with #; to satisfy both formats, but the real recommendation is to use a proper .env parsing library instead.

recent_posts.title: Why closing your open source repos won't protect you from AI hacking threats
recent_posts.summary: In response to concerns about Anthropic's Claude Mythos AI model being a powerful hacking tool, the author argues that open source developers should not close their repositories. Key reasons: open source code has already been ingested by AI training pipelines, most vulnerabilities exist in dependencies and supply chains rather than custom code, and closed-source systems are equally vulnerable to analysis. The author cites the UK AI Safety Institute's evaluation of Claude Mythos and NCSC guidance, neither of which recommend closing open source projects.

recent_posts.title: How spammers use fake conversational comment threads to sneak past filters
recent_posts.summary: A blog author describes a sophisticated spam technique where three AI-generated comments appear as a conversational thread, with the spam link buried in the middle reply. The comments came from the same IP, were spaced exactly 3 minutes apart, and used no URLs in the username fields to avoid detection. The author notes that purely technical anti-spam measures have limits, as spammers are economically motivated to circumvent them while barriers discourage genuine commenters.

recent_posts.title: Better TTS on Linux
recent_posts.summary: eSpeak is the default TTS engine on Linux but sounds robotic and dated. Piper is a modern, open-source, local-first TTS alternative that runs well on modest hardware without requiring cloud services or GPUs. The easiest way to install it is via Pied, a simple GUI that lets you browse and install voice accents, and automatically configures speech-dispatcher so the new voice works system-wide with accessibility services and apps like Firefox.

recent_posts.title: Book Review: Up - A scientist's guide to the magic above us by Dr Lucy Rogers
recent_posts.summary: A personal review of 'Up' by Dr Lucy Rogers, a science book exploring atmospheric and celestial phenomena above us. The reviewer praises its accessible tone, personal anecdotes, and encouragement of citizen science. Highlights include the author's hands-on fieldwork across tornado alley and the Vatican Archives, and the book's ability to rekindle curiosity about the natural world.

recent_posts.title: Reprojecting Dual Fisheye Videos to Equirectangular (LG 360)
recent_posts.summary: A practical guide to converting dual fisheye MP4 videos from the LG 360 Camera into equirectangular format for playback in VLC and YouTube. The process uses ffmpeg's v360 filter with a field-of-view value of 189° (determined by trial and error) to minimize lens overlap artifacts. Since ffmpeg doesn't write spherical metadata, exiftool is used separately to tag the output file as equirectangular. A combined one-liner using libx265 encoding and exiftool metadata injection is provided as the final solution.

recent_posts.title: Book Review: How To Kill A Witch - A Guide For The Patriarchy by Claire Mitchell and Zoe Venditozzi
recent_posts.summary: A review of 'How To Kill A Witch - A Guide For The Patriarchy' by Claire Mitchell and Zoe Venditozzi, a spin-off from the Witches of Scotland podcast. The book covers the Scottish Witch Trials, examining whether witchcraft accusations were genuine beliefs or tools of oppression against women. The reviewer praises the visceral historical descriptions and illustrations, but finds the author-centric podcast-style writing somewhat distracting and dislikes the imagined monologues from historical figures. A minor factual nitpick is raised about the book's misuse of historical life expectancy statistics. The book concludes with a sobering note that witch trial dynamics persist in parts of the modern world.
